'''Shirley Ellen Schwartz'''<ref name=":1" /> or '''Ellen Shirley Schwartz'''<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=http://obits.mlive.com/obituaries/annarbor/obituary.aspx?pid=180144817|title=Ellen Shirley Schwartz Ph.D. Obituary|date=2016-05-29|work=[[Ann Arbor News]]|access-date=2017-03-16}}</ref> (August 26, 1935 – May 8, 2016) was an American chemist and research scientist at [[General Motors]], specializing in the study and development of [[Lubricant|industrial lubricants]] and automobile [[Motor oil#Maintenance|oil change]] indicator systems. She was inducted into the [[Michigan Women's Hall of Fame]] in 1996 for her accomplishments in the field of chemistry.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.michiganwomenshalloffame.org/Images/Schwartz,%20Shirley%20E..pdf|title=Michigan Women's Hall of Fame: Shirley E. Schwartz|publisher=[[Michigan Women's Hall of Fame]]|access-date=2017-03-15}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Born '''Ellen Shirley Eckwall''' in [[Detroit]], Schwartz grew up in the Detroit suburb of [[Pleasant Ridge, Michigan|Pleasant Ridge]], and graduated from Lincoln High School in [[Ferndale, Michigan|Ferndale]].<ref name=":2" /> She earned three academic degrees in chemistry. She attended the [[University of Michigan]] where she received her Bachelor of Science degree in chemistry in 1957. Schwartz then enrolled at [[Wayne State University]] and earned her master's degree 1962 and her doctorate in 1970.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" />

==Career==
After teaching at [[Oakland Community College]] and the [[Detroit Institute of Technology]], Schwartz began working at [[BASF|BASF Corporation]] in [[Wyandotte, Michigan]], where she developed an industrial lubricant that, by virtue of being primarily water, reduced the amount of oil and consequently pollution.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> She then spent over 18 years working at General Motors, where she was senior research scientist, working in Research and Development Operations at the [[General Motors Technical Center]] in [[Warren, Michigan]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|year=1999|title=SAE Names 16 New Fellows|journal=PR Newswire|volume=Jan. 7, 1999|id={{ProQuest| }}}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> During her career she came to hold more than 20 patents, and authored 173 technical papers. From 1989 to 2003 she wrote a regular column titled ''Love Letters to Lubrication Engineers'' in the journal of the [[Society of Tribologists and Lubrication Engineers]], and was remembered in a 2016 memorial in that journal as "the mother of the oil life monitor found in most GM cars, which is responsible for not having to change oil nearly as often as we did previously, or conversely, not ruining your engine if you don't change it often enough."<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Baker|first=Ed and Jean|year=2016|title=Remembering Shirley Schwartz: Renaissance woman, STLE member and pioneer of women in science passes away at 81|journal=Tribology & Lubrication Technology|volume=72|issue=7 |pages=72|via=EbscoHost}}</ref><ref name=":2" />

When presenting her with an achievement award in 1999, the [[Society of Women Engineers]] summarized Dr. Schwartz's career thusly:

"Dr. Schwartz has examined engine oil degradation; wear, corrosion, and [[elastomer]] durability in engines; the effects of [[Methanol fuel|methanol]] and [[ethanol fuel]] on engines; and lubricants for air conditioners that use alternative refrigerants (other than [[Dichlorodifluoromethane|Freon R12]]). Her work in these areas have been targeted towards:
* obtaining the maximum useful life of engine oil
* finding acceptable ways to use [[alternative energy]] sources
* developing refrigerant systems that will not hurt the earth's [[ozone layer]]"<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://societyofwomenengineers.swe.org/images/AwardRecipients/pr_achieveawrd_schwartz.pdf|title=1999 Achievement Award Dr. Shirley E. Schwartz|website=Society of Women Engineers}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Schwartz was named a fellow of the [[SAE International|Society of Automotive Engineers]] in 1999<ref name=":3" /> and was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2000 "for contributions to lubrication engineering and for enriching the technical community through free-lance writing."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nae.edu/30433.aspx|title=NAE Website – Dr. Shirley E. Schwartz|access-date=2017-03-16}}</ref> She additionally received many industry awards:<ref name=":0" />
* General Motors Kettering Award (1988): Awarded for computer-based method that assesses engine oil degradation as a function of oil temperature and displays the remaining life of the oil for the vehicle<ref>{{Cite journal|last=PR Newswire Association LLC|year=1989|title=GM honors inventors|journal=PR Newswire|volume=Jan. 24, 1989|via=General OneFile}}</ref>          
* General Motors McCuen Award (1993)
* Gold Award from the [[Engineering Society of Detroit]] (1989)
* Wilbur Deutsch Memorial Award from the [[Society of Tribologists and Lubrication Engineers]] (1987)
* Colwell Award (1992) from the [[Society of Automotive Engineers]]
* Distinguished Speaker Award (1995) from the [[Society of Automotive Engineers]]

==Personal life==
Schwartz married her husband, Ron Schwartz, in 1957.<ref name=":2" />
